signals: anything asking for nodes at the same depth together
constraints: Up to 2000 nodes, so any O(n) traversal is fine; the size is small enough that even a per-level reversal or insert-at-front is irrelevant. Tree problems rarely care about n; the hint is the structure, not the size.
confusable: Beginners try to design a special bottom-up traversal or recurse by height first; just run the normal top-down BFS and reverse the list of levels, or insert each level at index 0.
variants: Zigzag order (103): same BFS, reverse every other level
Right side view (199): keep the last node of each level
Average / largest value per level (637, 515): aggregate over each level list instead of storing it

signals: "height-balanced" / heights of left and right subtrees
a property that must hold at EVERY node
answer depends on a value computed from children (height, size, sum)
constraints: 5000 nodes rules out the naive approach of recomputing height at every node (O(n^2) in a skewed tree would still pass here, but the intended answer is O(n)). Post-order returning height plus a sentinel is O(n) and works for any n.
confusable: The obvious top-down version calls height() from every node, which recomputes subtrees repeatedly; post-order (compute children first, combine, return upward) checks height and balance in one pass.
variants: Diameter of binary tree (543): same post-order height with a global max of left+right
Maximum depth (104): the height helper alone
Any 'is the tree X' property where X depends on children: return a tuple (valid, height/size/min/max) per subtree

signals: stop at the first node satisfying a condition ("leaf")
unweighted tree or graph where the first hit is the answer
constraints: Up to 1e5 nodes, so O(n) is required and recursion depth can hit 1e5 on a skewed tree; BFS avoids stack overflow and also terminates early, which DFS cannot.
confusable: Copying maximum depth as min(left, right) + 1 is wrong when a node has only one child (a missing child is not a leaf); also DFS must explore everything while BFS can stop at the first leaf.
variants: Maximum depth (104): DFS/post-order is natural since you must see everything
Nearest leaf to a given node (742): convert to graph and BFS from that node
Any 'minimum number of steps' in an unweighted structure: BFS

signals: "sum of values along the path equals target"
yes/no existence question on a tree
a leaf is explicitly defined as a node with no children
constraints: 5000 nodes with values in [-1000, 1000] means plain O(n) DFS; no pruning on sign is possible since negatives exist, so you must reach every leaf in the worst case.
confusable: Checking remaining == 0 at any node (including internal ones or null children) is the classic mistake; the check must happen only at a leaf, and negative values mean you cannot prune when remaining goes below 0.
variants: Path Sum II (113): return every matching path, so carry the path and backtrack
Path Sum III (437): paths need not start at root or end at leaf, use prefix-sum hash map along the DFS
Sum root-to-leaf numbers (129): carry an accumulator down instead of subtracting

signals: enumerate every solution rather than count or test
path built from root state that must be undone when returning
constraints: 5000 nodes and output size can be large, but each path is at most tree height; append-recurse-pop keeps it O(n * h) worst case. Values in [-1000, 1000] so no pruning by sign.
confusable: Copying the path list at every call (path + [val]) works but costs O(h) per node; the backtracking discipline is push, recurse, pop with a single shared list, copying only when a leaf matches.
variants: Path Sum (112): existence only, drop the path bookkeeping
Binary tree paths (257): same enumeration with no sum condition
Subsets / combinations (78, 77): identical push/recurse/pop shape on an array

signals: "number of distinct subsequences" of one string equal to another
two strings to align (s and t)
subsequence means skip allowed in s, no skip in t
constraints: Both lengths up to 1000, so an O(|s| * |t|) = 1e6 table is the intended solution; anything exponential over subsequences is out. Use a 2D DP or a 1D rolling row over t.
confusable: Looks like LCS or edit distance, but the transition is asymmetric: you may always skip s[i], and only when s[i] == t[j] may you also consume both; carrying the built string or generating subsequences blows up exponentially.
variants: Is Subsequence (392): existence only, greedy two pointers
Edit Distance (72) / LCS (1143): same two-string (i, j) grid with different transitions
Number of matching subsequences (792): many small t's against one s, use bucketed pointers

signals: "next pointer" to the node on the same level
"perfect binary tree" / every parent has two children
constraints: Up to 2^12 - 1 nodes, so any O(n) works; the follow-up asks for O(1) extra space, and the perfect-tree guarantee is exactly what makes the level-walking trick via existing next pointers possible.
confusable: Beginners reach for a queue-based BFS with a level list, which is fine but O(w) space; the perfect-tree constraint is a hint that the previous level's next pointers already give you the traversal order for free.
variants: Version II (117): tree not perfect, use a dummy head per level
Level order traversal (102): same BFS without linking
Cousins in binary tree (993): compare depth and parent instead of linking

signals: "next pointer" to the next right node
link nodes across a level left to right
O(1) space follow-up on a tree
constraints: 6000 nodes, O(n) BFS is fine. The absence of the perfect-tree guarantee means the child-linking must handle missing children, which is why a dummy head and a tail pointer per level are used for the O(1)-space version.
confusable: Reusing the version-I trick (node.left.next = node.right, node.right.next = node.next.left) breaks when children are missing; either fall back to queue BFS or build each next level with a dummy head.
variants: Version I (116): perfect tree lets you skip the dummy head
Right side view (199): last node of each level is the one whose next is null
Flatten a linked-list of levels: same dummy-head chaining idea

signals: "buy" on one day, "sell" on a later day, one transaction
maximize difference a[j] - a[i] with i < j
single pass with a running min or max
constraints: 1e5 prices rules out checking every (i, j) pair (1e10); one pass tracking the running minimum is O(n). Prices are non-negative and small, but that does not matter for the approach.
confusable: It looks like a max-minus-min problem, but the max must come AFTER the min; also it is not Kadane on prices, it is Kadane on daily differences, which is the same as the running-min trick.
variants: Stock II (122): unlimited transactions, sum every positive daily difference
Stock III / IV (123, 188): at most k transactions, DP over states (transactions, holding)
Stock with cooldown / fee (309, 714): state-machine DP

signals: "path" in a tree that "does not need to pass through the root"
path may bend at a node (left + node + right)
maximize a value over all paths
negative values allowed so subtrees can be discarded
constraints: 3e4 nodes and values in [-1000, 1000]; O(n) post-order is required and negatives are the whole point: you must clamp a child's contribution to 0 rather than always including it.
confusable: Beginners return left + node + right up the recursion, which lets a path fork twice; the value returned upward must be the best single-branch gain, while the forked sum only updates the global answer.
variants: Diameter of binary tree (543): same shape with edge counts instead of sums
Longest univalue path (687): same shape with a condition on equal values
Longest path in a tree with a constraint on the bend (e.g. zigzag 1372): return per-direction values

signals: in-place check on a string without building a filtered copy
constraints: 2e5 characters means O(n) time; building a filtered lowercase string is also O(n) and passes, but the two-pointer version is O(1) extra space, which is the point of the pattern.
confusable: Filtering and comparing to the reverse is the easy way and works, but it uses O(n) extra space; also forgetting that digits count as alphanumeric.
variants: Valid Palindrome II (680): allow one deletion, branch once when a mismatch is found
Longest palindromic substring (5): expand from the center rather than from the ends
Reverse vowels / reverse words: same two-ended pointer motion with a skip condition

signals: longest run of x, x+1, x+2...
constraints: 1e5 elements and values up to 1e9: sorting gives O(n log n) which passes but violates the stated O(n); values too large to index a counting array, so a hash set is the tool. Starting only from run starts keeps it linear.
confusable: Sort-then-scan is the reflex and is accepted, but the problem explicitly asks for O(n); also walking up from every element without the 'x - 1 not in set' check degrades to O(n^2).
variants: Sort then scan adjacent differences: if O(n log n) is allowed
Union-Find on x and x+1: same idea, more machinery
Longest consecutive sequence in a binary tree (298): DFS carrying the run length

signals: accumulate a value along the path (digits, product, string)
the accumulator is built top-down, the total is summed bottom-up
constraints: At most 1000 nodes and depth <= 10 guarantees the numbers fit in a 32-bit int; plain O(n) DFS, recursion depth trivially safe.
confusable: Collecting all paths as lists and then converting is O(n * h) extra work; carry the running number as a parameter (curr * 10 + val) and only materialize it at leaves.
variants: Path Sum (112): same top-down accumulator with subtraction instead of digit append
Binary tree paths (257): accumulate a string instead of a number
Sum of root-to-leaf binary numbers (1022): curr * 2 + val

signals: grid with regions that touch the "edge" or "border"
constraints: m, n <= 200 so a full O(mn) flood fill (40k cells) is trivial; recursion depth can reach 40k on a large 'O' region, so iterative DFS/BFS is safer in Python.
confusable: Flood-filling each interior region and checking whether it touches the border is correct but awkward; invert the question: flood from the border to mark what is safe, then everything unmarked is captured.
variants: Number of enclaves (1020): same border flood, count unmarked land
Pacific Atlantic water flow (417): flood from two borders and intersect
Number of islands (200): count components without the border condition

signals: each piece must satisfy a predicate (palindrome)
choose a cut point, recurse on the rest
constraints: s.length <= 16 is the giveaway: 2^15 possible cut sets, so exponential backtracking is intended. Precomputing an isPalindrome[i][j] table (16x16) makes each check O(1).
confusable: Looks like it wants DP because of 'palindrome' and 'partition', but the ask is to enumerate ALL partitions, which is inherently exponential; DP only helps for counting or minimizing.
variants: Palindrome Partitioning II (132): minimum cuts, now it IS a DP
Word Break II (140): same cut-and-recurse with a dictionary predicate
Restore IP addresses (93): partition into exactly 4 valid pieces

signals: nodes reference each other (neighbors, random pointers)
graph may have cycles so plain recursion would loop
constraints: At most 100 nodes and the graph is connected, so O(V + E) DFS or BFS is trivial; the constraint about no self-loops and unique values just simplifies the map keys.
confusable: Creating the clone after recursing into neighbors causes infinite recursion on cycles; the clone must be created and stored in the map BEFORE visiting neighbors.
variants: Copy list with random pointer (138): same old-to-new map on a linked list
Clone a tree: no map needed since there are no cycles
Clone N-ary tree (1490): identical, children instead of neighbors

signals: "constant extra space" demanded together with linear time
XOR identities x ^ x = 0, x ^ 0 = x
constraints: 3e4 elements and the explicit O(1)-space requirement kills the hash map/set approach even though it passes; XOR is the only way to meet both bounds.
confusable: A counter or set is the natural first thought and is accepted, but it uses O(n) space; the 'exactly twice' guarantee is the hint that XOR cancellation works.
variants: Single Number II (137): every other element appears three times, count bits mod 3
Single Number III (260): two singles, XOR all then split by a set bit
Missing number (268): XOR indices against values

constraints: 1e4 nodes, so even a visited-set O(n) approach passes; the follow-up asks for O(1) memory, which is what slow/fast delivers.
confusable: Storing visited nodes in a set works but costs O(n) space; also checking fast.next is null before fast.next.next is the usual crash.
variants: Linked List Cycle II (142): find the cycle entry with the second phase
Happy number (202): the same detection on an implicit sequence
Find the duplicate number (287): treat array values as next pointers

signals: "return the node where the cycle begins"
find the entry point, not just existence
duplicate value in an array of 1..n interpreted as a pointer
constraints: 1e4 nodes, O(n) time; the 'do not modify' rule blocks marking nodes and the O(1)-space follow-up blocks the set, leaving Floyd's two-phase walk.
confusable: After detecting a cycle with slow/fast, beginners stop or count cycle length; the trick is resetting one pointer to head and moving both one step until they meet at the entry.
variants: Linked List Cycle (141): existence only, phase one
Find the duplicate number (287): same two-phase algorithm on array indices
Intersection of two linked lists (160): different two-pointer trick, not a cycle

signals: interleave front and back of a list: L0, Ln, L1, Ln-1
"may not modify the values" only the nodes
needs the middle and the reversed second half
in-place rearrangement of a singly linked list
constraints: 5e4 nodes; the array-of-nodes approach is O(n) space and passes, but the intended O(1)-space solution combines three linked-list primitives: find middle, reverse, merge.
confusable: Dumping nodes into an array and re-linking by index is easy but O(n) extra space; the constant-space route is a composition of slow/fast midpoint, in-place reverse, and alternate merge.
variants: Palindrome linked list (234): same middle + reverse, then compare instead of merge
Reverse linked list (206) and middle of linked list (876): the two building blocks
Odd-even linked list (328): a different in-place re-linking pattern

signals: need ordering by recency plus keyed lookup
constraints: 2e5 calls with capacity up to 3000: an O(capacity) scan per operation would be 6e8, too slow; the O(1) requirement forces hash map plus doubly linked list (or an ordered dict).
confusable: Using a plain list or array to track recency makes moving an item to the front O(n); a doubly linked list gives O(1) unlink, and the map points directly at nodes.
variants: LFU cache (460): frequency buckets, each a doubly linked list
Design HashMap / HashSet (706, 705): hashing without recency
Any 'most recently used' or 'time-ordered eviction' design: same map + ordered list

signals: O(n log n) time with O(1) or O(log n) space follow-up
no random access so quicksort/heap are awkward
constraints: 5e4 nodes: O(n^2) insertion sort is ~2.5e9 comparisons, too slow; O(n log n) merge sort is required and merge sort is the natural choice because linked lists merge in O(1) extra space.
confusable: Copying values to an array, sorting, and writing back is O(n) extra space; also quicksort on a linked list is painful because partitioning needs random access.
variants: Merge two sorted lists (21): the merge step alone
Merge k sorted lists (23): divide and conquer over lists or a heap
Insertion sort list (147): the O(n^2) baseline

signals: compare mid to an endpoint to decide which half is sorted
constraints: n <= 5000 means a linear scan passes, but the statement explicitly demands O(log n), so binary search on the rotation is intended; unique values guarantee the mid-vs-right comparison is decisive.
confusable: Standard binary search needs a monotonic predicate; here nums[mid] < nums[right] is the monotonic test, not nums[mid] < target, and comparing to the left end is ambiguous.
variants: Version II (154): duplicates allowed, shrink right by one when nums[mid] == nums[right]
Search in rotated sorted array (33): find a target by identifying the sorted half
Peak element (162): binary search on a different monotone-ish predicate

signals: "stack" with an extra query ("min", "max") in "constant time"
aggregate must be undone on pop
constraints: 3e4 calls and the explicit O(1)-per-op requirement rules out scanning the stack for the min on each getMin (O(n) each); an auxiliary min stack costs O(1) per op and O(n) space.
confusable: Keeping a single running minimum breaks on pop (you cannot recover the previous min); the fix is a parallel stack (or pairs) storing the min at each depth.
variants: Max stack (716): same idea plus a popMax, needs a treemap or lazy deletion
Min queue: two min stacks forming a queue
Stack with O(1) frequency lookup (895 Maximum Frequency Stack): stacks per frequency

signals: "maximum difference between successive elements in sorted form"
"linear time and linear extra space" demanded
pigeonhole: n - 1 buckets guarantee the answer straddles a bucket gap
constraints: 1e5 elements with values up to 1e9: comparison sort is O(n log n) and passes, but the stated linear-time requirement points to radix sort or bucket sort; values up to 1e9 rule out counting sort by value.
confusable: Sorting then scanning is the obvious answer and is accepted, but it is not linear; the bucket trick works only because the maximum gap is at least (max - min) / (n - 1), so no answer lies inside a bucket.
variants: Contains duplicate III (220): buckets of width t to test near-equality
Radix sort: another linear-time route for bounded integers
Minimum absolute difference (1200): sort then scan, no trick needed

signals: moving one end changes the sum monotonically
constraints: 3e4 elements, O(n^2) is borderline and the O(1)-space rule blocks the hash map; the sorted guarantee is what makes the opposite-ends two-pointer sweep O(n) and space-free.
confusable: Reaching for the hash map from Two Sum (1) ignores the sortedness and violates the space constraint; binary search per element also works but is O(n log n).
variants: Two Sum (1): unsorted, use a hash map
3Sum / 4Sum (15, 18): sort then fix one element and run this two-pointer inside
Count pairs with sum less than target: same pointers, add (j - i) to the count

constraints: 5e4 elements with values up to 1e9: a hash map count is O(n) time and space and passes; the strict-majority guarantee is what makes Boyer-Moore voting correct in O(1) space.
confusable: Counting with a hash map or sorting and taking the middle element both work, but the 'more than half' guarantee is a hint that pairwise cancellation leaves the majority standing without any extra memory.
variants: Majority Element II (229): more than n/3, keep two candidates
Without the guarantee: run voting then verify with a second count pass
Sort and return nums[n // 2]: O(n log n) alternative

signals: next() and hasNext() must be lazy
produce sorted values one at a time from a BST
constraints: 1e5 nodes and 1e5 calls: flattening to an array is O(n) memory and passes, but the stated goal is O(h) memory with amortized O(1) next(), which is exactly the left-spine stack.
confusable: Doing a full in-order traversal into a list in the constructor is the shortcut and violates the O(h) intent; the stack version pushes only the left spine and lazily expands right subtrees.
variants: Kth smallest in BST (230): the same stack, stop after k pops
Peeking iterator (284): wrap any iterator with a one-item buffer
Flatten nested list iterator (341): lazy stack over nested structures

signals: maximize a sum with a spacing constraint
optimal answer for prefix i depends on prefixes i-1 and i-2
constraints: n <= 100 and values <= 400: tiny, so even exponential recursion with memo passes; the point is the O(n) recurrence with two rolling variables.
confusable: Greedy (rob every other house, or compare odd vs even sums) fails on inputs like [2, 1, 1, 2]; the take/skip decision needs DP.
variants: House Robber II (213): circular street, run twice excluding first or last
House Robber III (337): tree version, return (rob, skip) per subtree
Delete and earn (740): bucket by value, then this exact recurrence

signals: one representative per level (first, last, max, average)
constraints: Up to 100 nodes, size is irrelevant; the level-by-level structure is the whole hint. Either BFS keeping the last of each level or DFS visiting right first and recording the first node at each new depth.
confusable: Following only right children misses nodes visible through a longer left branch; you need all levels, not the rightmost path.
variants: Left side view: first node per level or DFS left-first
Find largest value in each tree row (515): same BFS with max
Bottom-left value (513): last level's first node

signals: mark visited by mutating the grid
constraints: 300 x 300 = 9e4 cells so O(mn) BFS/DFS is fine; recursive DFS can reach 9e4 depth on a grid full of land, which is why iterative BFS or a raised recursion limit matters in Python.
confusable: Counting every '1' cell, or scanning rows without flood-filling, overcounts; each new unvisited land cell must trigger a full component sink so it is counted once.
variants: Max area of island (695): same flood fill returning component size
Number of islands II (305): incremental additions, use Union-Find
Surrounded regions (130): flood from the border instead

signals: "repeat the process until" it reaches a fixed value "or loops endlessly"
detect a cycle in an implicit sequence
constraints: n up to 2^31 - 1, but the digit-square sum of any such number is at most 9^2 * 10 = 810, so the sequence quickly enters a small range; a seen-set is tiny, and slow/fast gives O(1) space.
confusable: Fearing the huge input, beginners look for a math formula; the sequence collapses into a small range, so plain cycle detection (set or Floyd) is all that is needed.
variants: Linked list cycle (141): the same Floyd detection on pointers
Find the duplicate number (287): Floyd on array-index sequence
Collatz-style 'does this process terminate' questions: seen-set with a bound argument

signals: sub-step of many harder list problems
constraints: 5000 nodes; iterative O(n) with O(1) space is the standard; recursion also works at this depth but would overflow near 1e5 in Python.
confusable: Losing the rest of the list by overwriting curr.next before saving it; also recursion is elegant but the iterative three-pointer version is what other problems compose.
variants: Reverse Linked List II (92): reverse only positions left..right, needs a pre-node
Reverse nodes in k-group (25): reverse in chunks
Palindrome linked list (234) / Reorder list (143): reverse the second half

signals: "can you finish" / "is it possible" to order tasks
the question is really 'does the directed graph have a cycle'
constraints: 2000 nodes and 5000 edges means O(V + E) DFS or Kahn's is trivial; recursion depth up to 2000 is safe. Any algorithm that is polynomial passes, but cycle detection is the natural fit.
confusable: Using a single visited set (as in undirected graphs) reports false cycles on diamonds; directed cycle detection needs a separate 'on current path' state (three colors) or Kahn's in-degree counting.
variants: Course Schedule II (210): return the order, so use Kahn's or post-order reverse
Course Schedule IV (1462): reachability queries, Floyd-Warshall or DFS per node
Alien dictionary (269): build the edges from word pairs then topo-sort

constraints: Word length up to 2000 and 3e4 calls: each operation is O(L), total 6e7 character steps, fine; a hash set would make startsWith O(total characters) per query, which is the operation a trie makes cheap.
confusable: A hash set answers search in O(1) but startsWith requires scanning every word; the trie shares prefixes so both operations walk one path.
variants: Add and Search Words (211): wildcard '.' adds backtracking over children
Word Search II (212): trie plus grid DFS
Replace words / longest common prefix: walk the trie and stop at the first end flag

signals: shrinkable window: adding elements only increases the sum
optimize a window size under a monotone condition
constraints: 1e5 elements rules out O(n^2) enumeration; positive values make the sum monotone in the window, so a two-pointer window is O(n). The O(n log n) follow-up hints at prefix sums plus binary search.
confusable: If the array could contain zeros or negatives the window would not be monotonic; then you would need prefix sums with a monotonic deque (862) instead.
variants: Subarray sum equals k (560): exact sum with negatives, prefix sum + hash map
Shortest subarray with sum at least K (862): negatives allowed, prefix sums + monotonic deque
Longest subarray with sum <= target: same window, maximize instead

signals: produce a linear order of tasks
constraints: 2000 nodes and up to n(n-1) edges (~4e6), so O(V + E) Kahn's is needed and adjacency lists (not matrices per query) keep it linear; building the in-degree array is the key data structure.
confusable: Beginners try to sort courses by number of prerequisites or by DFS discovery order; neither is a topological order. Use in-degree peeling or reversed post-order.
variants: Course Schedule (207): yes/no version
Parallel courses (1136): number of BFS layers in Kahn's = minimum semesters
Sort items by groups respecting dependencies (1203): two-level topo sort

signals: "dots can be matched with any letter" / wildcard search
pattern matching over a set of strings
constraints: Word length <= 25 and at most 2 dots per query: a trie with at most 26^2 branching from the dots is small; 1e4 calls make even a naive per-word regex scan plausible, but the trie is intended.
confusable: A hash set cannot handle '.', and grouping words by length then scanning is O(words) per query; the trie limits the search to matching prefixes and only branches at dots.
variants: Implement Trie (208): no wildcards
Word Search II (212): trie plus DFS over a grid
Wildcard / regex matching (44, 10): pattern against ONE string, use DP

signals: top-k of a stream or array
constraints: 1e5 elements: full sort is O(n log n) and passes; a size-k min-heap is O(n log k), and quickselect is average O(n). Values in [-1e4, 1e4] also allow counting sort in O(n + range).
confusable: Sorting the whole array is the reflex; a heap of size k avoids ordering everything, and a max-heap of all n elements is the wrong heap direction for top-k.
variants: Kth largest in a stream (703): keep the size-k min-heap alive
Top K frequent elements (347): count first, then heap or bucket sort
K closest points (973): same heap keyed on distance

signals: no structure to exploit (unsorted, unbounded values)
constraints: 1e5 elements with values up to 1e9: nested loops are 1e10, too slow; values are too large for a boolean array, so a hash set (O(n)) or sort-then-adjacent (O(n log n)) is the way.
confusable: Comparing every pair is O(n^2); also sorting works but is slower than the set and destroys order if that matters.
variants: Contains Duplicate II (219): duplicate within k indices, sliding-window set
Contains Duplicate III (220): within k indices and value diff t, buckets or sorted container
Find all duplicates (442): values in 1..n let you mark in place

signals: apply the same local operation at every node
constraints: 100 nodes; trivially O(n) with any traversal. Recursion depth is not a concern.
confusable: Overthinking traversal order: the swap is local, so pre-order, post-order, or BFS all produce the same result; the only bug is forgetting to recurse into both children.
variants: Symmetric tree (101): compare a tree with its mirror instead of building it
Flip equivalent binary trees (951): compare allowing a swap at each node
Same tree (100): simultaneous traversal of two trees

constraints: 1e4 nodes and k <= n: a full in-order into a list is O(n) and passes; the iterative stack version stops after k pops, giving O(h + k), which matters for the follow-up with frequent queries.
confusable: Treating it like an array problem (heap or sort) ignores that the BST already provides sorted order via in-order; a heap is O(n log k) for nothing.
variants: BST iterator (173): the same lazy stack as a class
Kth largest: reverse in-order (right, node, left)
Frequent queries with modifications: augment nodes with subtree sizes

signals: compare the front with the back of a singly linked structure
constraints: 1e5 nodes: copying to an array is O(n) space and passes, but the O(1)-space follow-up forces the slow/fast middle plus in-place reversal of the second half.
confusable: The array copy is the easy answer; the constant-space version composes middle-finding and reversal, and must handle odd length by skipping the middle node.
variants: Reorder list (143): same middle + reverse, then merge
Valid palindrome (125): the two-pointer version on a string
Middle of the linked list (876) and reverse (206): the building blocks

signals: two target values, decide a direction
walk down from the root without recursion into both sides
constraints: 1e5 nodes and values up to 1e9 with unique values: the BST property gives O(h) without visiting the whole tree, and the iterative walk uses O(1) space; no need for parent pointers or paths.
confusable: Applying the general-tree LCA (recurse into both subtrees) works but is O(n) and ignores the BST property; the split point where p and q go in different directions is the answer.
variants: LCA of a binary tree (236): no ordering, post-order returning found nodes
LCA with parent pointers (1650): walk up like intersecting linked lists
Insert / search in a BST (701, 700): the same directional walk

signals: combine a left-side aggregate with a right-side aggregate
"O(n)" demanded on something that naively needs nested loops
constraints: 1e5 elements rules out O(n^2); values in [-30, 30] with the 32-bit guarantee means overflow is not the concern; the no-division rule forces prefix and suffix products rather than total / nums[i].
confusable: Dividing the total product by nums[i] is the reflex, breaks on zeros and is forbidden; prefix times suffix handles zeros naturally.
variants: Prefix sum (range sum query 303): the additive version
Trapping rain water (42): left-max and right-max arrays, same two-sided sweep
Minimum operations to make array equal / any 'value from both sides' problem: precompute left and right passes

signals: each element enters once and is evicted once
candidate maintenance with a monotone order
constraints: 1e5 elements with k up to n: recomputing the max per window is O(nk) = 1e10, too slow; a monotonic deque is O(n), and a heap with lazy deletion is O(n log n), also fine.
confusable: It is a sliding window, but the max is not maintainable by simple add/remove counters; a heap needs stale-index eviction, and the deque works only because dominated elements can be discarded forever.
variants: Shortest subarray with sum at least K (862): monotonic deque on prefix sums
Sliding window median (480): needs two heaps or a sorted container
Next greater element (496): monotonic stack, same discard logic without a window

signals: matrix "sorted" in each row AND each column
each comparison must eliminate a row or a column
constraints: 300 x 300 with values up to 1e9: the staircase walk is O(m + n) = 600 steps; per-row binary search is O(m log n) and also fine; brute force 9e4 also passes, so the intended pattern is judged by elegance, not the limits.
confusable: Treating it like Search a 2D Matrix I (74) and doing a single binary search fails because rows are not globally ordered; start at a corner where one direction increases and the other decreases.
variants: Search a 2D Matrix (74): rows globally sorted, one binary search over m*n
Kth smallest in a sorted matrix (378): binary search on value plus this staircase count
Count negatives in a sorted matrix (1351): same staircase for counting
